claims.claim: Sylvia Kelso judges the quoted opening paragraph of Always Coming Home to contain no rhythmic superfluities.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, "Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin", Paradoxa 21 (2009), pp. 7-22
claims.quote: Here there are no rhythmic superfluities

claims.claim: Sylvia Kelso states that the repeated splitting of rushes in the Tenar and Moss scene operates as a suite of variations marking pause and emphasis.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, "Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin", Paradoxa 21 (2009), pp. 7-22
claims.quote: a suite of variations to indicate pause and emphasis

claims.claim: Sylvia Kelso describes the rhythm of the Kalessin arrival passage in Tehanu as almost somnambulistically smooth, with an extraordinarily long second sentence whose commas weight the critical words.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, "Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin", Paradoxa 21 (2009), pp. 7-22
claims.quote: almost somnambulistically smooth, the second sentence extraordinarily long

claims.claim: Le Guin complains that writers taught 'show don't tell' are afraid to describe the world they have invented.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'On Rules of Writing, or, Riffing on Rechy' (Los Angeles Times, 2003), ursulakleguin.com
claims.quote: They’re afraid to describe the world they’ve invented.

claims.claim: Le Guin argues the narrator's voice, often called omniscient, is the most intimate voice of all rather than a distancing one.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'On Rules of Writing, or, Riffing on Rechy' (Los Angeles Times, 2003), ursulakleguin.com
claims.quote: it’s the most intimate voice of all

claims.claim: Le Guin defends narrative distance with the phrase that distance lends enchantment.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'On Rules of Writing, or, Riffing on Rechy' (Los Angeles Times, 2003), ursulakleguin.com

claims.claim: Le Guin criticises writers for abandoning the narrative past tense for what she calls the tight-focused, inflexible present tense.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'On Rules of Writing, or, Riffing on Rechy' (Los Angeles Times, 2003), ursulakleguin.com

claims.claim: Le Guin states flatly that stories are not shown but told.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1' (Book View Cafe, 2015)
claims.quote: stories are not shown, but told

claims.claim: Le Guin tells writers to distrust anybody who says fiction must use only limited third person.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1' (Book View Cafe, 2015)

claims.claim: Le Guin says the currently practiced limited third person gives a brilliant, narrow, simplifying intensity of vision, like a flashlight beam.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1' (Book View Cafe, 2015)
claims.quote: a brilliant, narrow, simplifying intensity of vision

claims.claim: Le Guin coins the term Macho Staccato for the contemporary avoidance of complex sentences.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1, Part 3' (Book View Cafe, 2015)
claims.quote: avoid complex sentences and write what I call Macho Staccato

claims.claim: Le Guin says the ideal is flexibility, a balance of different sentence lengths depending on what each sentence does.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1, Part 3' (Book View Cafe, 2015)
claims.quote: The ideal is flexibility, a balance of different sentence lengths

claims.claim: Le Guin says words are bodily, made with the body and the breath, so the rhythms of words are bodily rhythms.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'What Makes a Story' (c. 2007), ursulakleguin.com
claims.quote: the rhythms of words are bodily rhythms
